# Diagnosing Raw Fuel Smell and Rough Idle on a Post-Rebuild BMW E46

A raw fuel smell emanating from the exhaust pipe combined with a rough idle is a definitive indicator that unburned gasoline is passing through the combustion chamber and exiting via the tailpipe. In the context of a recently replaced engine with 8,900 miles and an illuminated check engine light, this is not merely a nuisance; it is a symptom of a lean or rich air/fuel mixture imbalance, misfiring cylinders, or a compromised sealing system. The fact that the car runs rough suggests the Engine Control Unit (ECU) cannot maintain stable combustion under load or idle conditions.

When an engine smells like gas, the primary suspect is often the ignition system failing to ignite the fuel mixture completely. If a spark plug is fouled, the coil pack is weak, or the ignition wires are degraded, the cylinder fires late or not at all. The ECU detects this via upstream oxygen sensors and attempts to compensate by enriching the mixture, but if the mechanical fault persists, raw fuel continues to escape. Another critical failure point in a high-mileage rebuild scenario is the PCV (Positive Crankcase Ventilation) system. If the crankcase breather is clogged or the valve is stuck open, excessive crankcase pressure can force oil vapors and unburned fuel back into the intake manifold, confusing the ECU's air-fuel ratio calculations.

### Investigating the Fuel Pressure Regulator

One specific component frequently overlooked in post-rebuild diagnostics is the fuel pressure regulator. On many BMW 3-series models, this unit is integrated directly onto the fuel rail or located near the high-pressure line. If the internal diaphragm ruptures, it allows excess fuel to bypass the injector return path and enter the intake manifold via the vacuum port. This creates a severe "rich" condition where there is simply too much fuel for the available air, resulting in black smoke, a strong gasoline odor, and rough running.

To diagnose this without disassembling the engine bay immediately, you can monitor live data streams using an OBD-II scanner that supports PID (Parameter Identification) reading. Look for the Short Term Fuel Trim (STFT) and Long Term Fuel Trim (LTFT). In a healthy system, these values should fluctuate between -10% and +10%. If you observe sustained positive trims (e.g., +20% or higher), the ECU is commanding injectors to close early to compensate for excess fuel in the manifold. This confirms a vacuum leak into the intake side of the regulator or a leaking injector.

### The Role of Exhaust Gas Recirculation and Sensors

Given that the check engine light is illuminated, the ECU has likely stored a Diagnostic Trouble Code (DTC). Codes related to oxygen sensors (P0130âP0167) or fuel system trims (P0171âP0174) are common. A stuck-open Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR) valve can also mimic these symptoms by allowing exhaust gases to enter the intake, diluting the air/fuel mixture and causing rough idle, though it typically smells more like burnt oil than raw gas. However, if the EGR passage is clogged with carbon from the initial engine replacement or previous operation, it creates a restriction that disrupts flow dynamics.

### Addressing the High-Mileage Context

The fact that this is a rebuilt engine with 89,000 miles introduces a variable: component wear versus installation error. While new parts should theoretically last longer, the mating surfaces and gaskets are critical. A blown head gasket can allow coolant into cylinders (causing white smoke) or exhaust gases into the cooling system, but it can also disrupt combustion stability if the compression seal is compromised. If the engine was assembled correctly but now exhibits these symptoms after 89k miles on a rebuild, consider that the initial "new" parts may have been lower quality than expected, or that the fuel pump itself is failing to maintain consistent pressure over time.

### Resolution Path

Before considering scrapping the vehicle, a systematic approach is required. Start by reading the freeze frame data from the ECU to see the exact conditions when the fault occurred. Clear the codes and perform a drive cycle to reset the adaptive learning values. If the fuel trim remains high, replace the fuel pressure regulator and inspect the injector return lines for leaks. Verify spark plug gap and ignition coil resistance with a multimeter. Only after ruling out sensor and injection issues should you investigate internal compression or valve timing again.

If the diagnostics confirm that the engine control strategy cannot be stabilized despite replacing standard wear items, and if the cost of further repair exceeds the vehicle's market value, then discontinuing the project is a rational economic decision. However, given the investment already made, methodically eliminating fuel delivery and ignition faults will likely resolve the smell and rough running without needing to junk the car.
